title: Infectious Diseases in Humans
seo_title: Secondary 4 Biology: Infectious Diseases in Humans Worksheets (O-Level 6093 with Answers)
standard_code: O-Level Biology (6093): Infectious Diseases in Humans
standard_text: Describe infectious diseases as caused by pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, using influenza and pneumococcal disease as examples, including their causes, transmission and symptoms; describe the body's defences, including physical barriers, phagocytosis and the production of antibodies by lymphocytes; distinguish between active and passive immunity; describe how vaccination works and the role of herd immunity; explain why antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses and how antibiotic resistance develops (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Biology 6093 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Biology worksheets on infectious diseases: pathogens, influenza, pneumococcal disease, body defences, antibodies, immunity, vaccines and antibiotics. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Vaccines make memory cells; antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses.
key_sub: Active immunity: your own antibodies. Passive: ready-made antibodies.
body_html:
How to think about it

The body fights pathogens in layers.

  • Barriers: skin, mucus and cilia, stomach acid, blood clotting.
  • Phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies specific to antigens and leave memory cells.
  • Vaccines contain weakened or dead pathogens or antigens. They give active immunity without the disease.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses. Overuse lets resistant bacteria survive and spread.
Example

Baby gets antibodies in breast milk.

ready-made antibodies

no memory cells

Answer: natural passive immunity

Example

Antibiotic for influenza?

influenza is a virus

Answer: no effect

Common mistakes

  • Saying antibiotics kill viruses.
  • Saying a vaccine contains antibodies.
  • Saying bacteria “become immune” to antibiotics.
  • Mixing up active and passive immunity.

faq.a: It contains dead or weakened pathogens or their antigens. Lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells, so if the real pathogen enters later, antibodies are made quickly before illness develops.

faq.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
faq.a: In active immunity the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells, so it lasts a long time. In passive immunity ready-made antibodies are received, so it acts at once but lasts only a short time.

faq.q: Why do antibiotics not work on viruses?
faq.a: Antibiotics damage structures or processes found in bacteria, such as cell walls. Viruses do not have these and reproduce inside host cells.

items.q: How is cholera mainly transmitted?
c: breathing in droplets from an infected person's cough
bacteria in soil entering a deep wound
items.e: Cholera: drinking water contaminated with faeces.

items.q: Can dengue fever be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: Dengue fever is caused by a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: How is food poisoning mainly transmitted?
c: bacteria in soil entering a deep wound
breathing in droplets from an infected person's cough
items.e: Food poisoning: eating food contaminated with bacteria.

items.q: Can cholera be treated with antibiotics?

items.e: Cholera is caused by a bacterium. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

c: droplets from the nose and throat of an infected person
items.e: Both are spread by droplets from the airways.

items.q: Which symptoms are typical of influenza?
c: a red rash and itching only
fever and chest pain; it can cause pneumonia, meningitis and blood infections
fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches and tiredness
items.e: Learn the main symptoms of each disease.

items.q: Which measures help to prevent or control pneumococcal disease?
c: a yearly influenza vaccine, covering the nose and mouth when coughing, and washing hands
the pneumococcal vaccine and good hygiene; it is treated with antibiotics
items.e: Vaccination and hygiene reduce spread.

items.q: What does a vaccine contain?
c: dead or weakened pathogens, or their antigens
items.e: It triggers an immune response without causing the disease.

items.q: What causes pneumococcal disease?

items.q: Can the common cold be treated with antibiotics?

items.q: Why must a new influenza vaccine be made each year?
c: The old vaccine stops working in the fridge.
The virus mutates, so its antigens change.
items.e: Memory cells may not recognise the new antigens.

c: a red rash and itching only
fever and chest pain; it can cause pneumonia, meningitis and blood infections
fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches and tiredness

items.q: How do hairs and mucus in the nose help defend the body?
c: It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: How does acid in the stomach help defend the body?
c: They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Trap particles that may contain pathogens”?
c: hairs and mucus in the nose
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is a pathogen?
items.e: Bacteria and viruses are pathogens.

items.q: Which is one way antibodies help to destroy pathogens? They…
c: turn the pathogen into a vaccine
digest the pathogen inside the lymphocyte
items.e: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes. They cause pathogens to clump together (agglutination), among other actions.

items.q: What role does the skin play in defending the body against pathogens?
c: a physical barrier that stops pathogens entering
make antibodies specific to the antigens on a pathogen
trap pathogens and sweep them up to the throat
seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter
items.e: The skin: a physical barrier that stops pathogens entering.

items.q: What role does mucus and cilia in the airways play in defending the body against pathogens?
c: make antibodies specific to the antigens on a pathogen
kills many pathogens in food and drink
seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter
trap pathogens and sweep them up to the throat
items.e: Mucus and cilia in the airways: trap pathogens and sweep them up to the throat.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Engulf and digest pathogens”?
c: hairs and mucus in the nose
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

c: a physical barrier that stops pathogens entering
seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter
kills many pathogens in food and drink
items.e: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach: kills many pathogens in food and drink.

items.q: Which defence has this role: “trap pathogens and sweep them up to the throat”?

items.q: Which is one way antibodies help to destroy pathogens? They…
c: break open the cell walls of bacteria
turn the pathogen into a vaccine
digest the pathogen inside the lymphocyte
items.e: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes. They break open the cell walls of bacteria, among other actions.

items.q: Which is one way antibodies help to destroy pathogens? They…
c: digest the pathogen inside the lymphocyte
turn the pathogen into a vaccine
attach to pathogens, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf
items.e: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes. They attach to pathogens, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf, among other actions.

items.q: Why do antibiotics not work against influenza?
c: Influenza is caused by a virus, and antibiotics act only on bacteria.
items.e: Antiviral drugs are different.

items.q: How do antitoxins help defend the body?
c: They neutralise toxins made by bacteria.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What role does blood clotting play in defending the body against pathogens?
c: kills many pathogens in food and drink
a physical barrier that stops pathogens entering
seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter
items.e: Blood clotting: seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter.

items.q: How do cilia in the trachea and bronchi help defend the body?
c: They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
It acts as a barrier and makes antimicrobial secretions.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: Why should a patient finish the whole course of antibiotics?
c: to kill all the bacteria, so resistant ones are less likely to survive and multiply
items.e: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive.

items.q: Why does overuse of antibiotics in farming worry doctors?
c: It increases the chance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria spreading to humans.
It makes animals immune to viruses.
items.e: Resistant bacteria are harder to treat.

items.q: A person recovers from influenza and makes memory cells. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Which disease is mainly spread by bites from infected Aedes mosquitoes?
items.e: Dengue fever: bites from infected Aedes mosquitoes.

items.q: You have chickenpox and recover, and do not catch it again. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: A nurse is given a booster dose of the tetanus vaccine. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Why is passive immunity short-lived?
c: The person makes too many antibodies.
The pathogens are all killed at once.
The antibodies given are broken down and no memory cells are made.
items.e: Active immunity lasts much longer.

items.q: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria arise?
c: The patient becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
A random mutation makes some bacteria resistant; they survive the antibiotic and multiply.
items.e: This is natural selection.

items.q: A person cuts a finger, and the wound becomes red and swollen. Which cells move to the area to engulf bacteria?
items.e: This is part of the inflammatory response.

items.q: What is an antigen?
c: a type of white blood cell
a molecule on the surface of a pathogen that triggers the making of antibodies
items.e: Each pathogen has its own antigens.

items.q: Which disease is mainly spread by breathing in droplets from an infected person's cough?
items.e: Tuberculosis: breathing in droplets from an infected person's cough.

items.q: A fetus receives antibodies across the placenta. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Why does a vaccinated person not become ill when infected?
c: The vaccine kills all pathogens in the air.
Memory cells make antibodies quickly, before the pathogen can multiply.
The vaccine stays in the blood for ever as antibodies.
items.e: The secondary response is faster and larger.

items.q: A newborn baby is protected for a few months by antibodies that crossed the placenta from its mother. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: What is herd immunity?
c: When most people are vaccinated, the disease cannot spread easily, protecting those who are not immune.
items.e: This protects babies and people who cannot be vaccinated.

items.q: A graph shows antibody levels after a first and second dose of a vaccine. Why is the second response faster and higher?
c: The person has more red blood cells.
Memory cells from the first dose recognise the antigen and make antibodies quickly.
The pathogen is weaker the second time.
items.e: This is the basis of booster doses.

items.q: Which is one way antibodies help to destroy pathogens? They…
c: digest the pathogen inside the lymphocyte
turn the pathogen into a vaccine
items.e: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes. They neutralise toxins made by bacteria, among other actions.

items.q: How does wearing a mask reduce the spread of influenza?
c: It stops many droplets from the nose and mouth spreading to others.
It kills viruses in the blood.
items.e: Hand washing also helps.

items.q: Which disease is mainly spread by drinking water contaminated with faeces?
items.e: Cholera: drinking water contaminated with faeces.

items.q: A baby drinks colostrum, the first breast milk, rich in antibodies. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: How is influenza mainly spread?
c: droplets from coughs and sneezes, and touching contaminated surfaces
items.e: Both are spread by droplets from the airways.

items.q: Why are elderly people in Singapore encouraged to receive the pneumococcal vaccine?
